Task 4: Gen-2 prototype characterization and integration experiments Task Summary: Under this task, NET Energy and its OEM partners will fabricate prototypes of the PCM thermal storage modules and incorporate them into the existing HVAC system and deliver them to NREL. NREL will characterize the performance of these prototypes in its laboratory, share these results with NET Energy, and use the results to validate or update their numerical models. The model described in Task 3 was validated with a stacked microchannel TES heat exchanger coupled to two glycol streams. The microchannel heat exchangers carry hot and cold propylene glycol - water through the component (Figure 16). Each array contains 9 tubes containing 135 individual microchannel ports with hydraulic diameters of 1.3 mm. The flow is split evenly into the microchannel ports by a common manifold. Thermal paste was added between the two arrays to reduce the contact resistance. Rectangular slabs (41.9 cm × 25.9 cm × 3.6 cm) of a graphite/tetradecane PCC are placed above and below the microchannel arrays. We found that tetradecane leaked out of the graphite material when cycled, so each slab was encapsulated in a heat-sealed Mylar bag. The bag increases the surface resistance but avoids the loss of capacity over time. 17 This report is available at no cost from the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL) at www.nrel.gov/publications. Figure 16: The microchannel heat exchanger used in the model validation experiments. Each microchannel array is attached to a common manifold that distributes the refrigerant to the microchannel ports. The microchannel tubes are bent at a 45-degree angle at both ends to allow room for the manifolds. The PCC slabs are placed above and below these microchannel arrays to provide thermal storage. The TES heat exchanger (“test section”) was placed in the facility shown in Figure 17. The inlet temperature and flow rate of the glycol mixture is controlled using constant temperature circulating baths (Fisher Scientific 6200 R35), a 1-kW external heater (Watlow FLUENT) and a DC variable speed diaphragm pump. The hot fluid loop (or discharge loop) can add heat to the cold loop and/or the PCC by supplying fluid at a constant inlet temperature (controlled with the temperature bath) or a constant power. For all constant power tests, the fluid temperature difference was set at 4.5°C and the flow rate was varied to achieve the desired heat transfer rate. The cold loop (or charge loop) can remove heat from the discharge loop and/or the PCC by supplying a constant temperature fluid to the test section inlet (controlled with the temperature bath). Pressure was applied to the top of the test section with a screw clamp to improve the thermal contact between the channel walls and the PCC. The tests were run with 4 psi of applied pressure, which was measured with a load cell (Omega LC304-5K). We evaluated the performance of the test section at a variety of charge and discharge rates.
